title: Portrait of Engalo
creator: Joey Lawrence (Joey L.)
datePrecision: year supported by photographer-published image metadata; exact timestamp not independently corroborated
body:
In 2008, Joey Lawrence photographed Engalo, a Mursi woman in Ethiopia’s Lower Omo Valley. White markings cover her face and shoulders, and light picks out her lip plate against the muted background. Lawrence made the series as posed colour portraits, using studio lighting. He wanted the people he photographed to appear as contemporaries, rather than inhabitants of a world outside modern life.

For Mursi women, a lip plate can express beauty, adulthood and belonging. It sits inside a pierced and stretched lower lip and can be removed. Women differ in whether they adopt the practice and how far they stretch their lips. The procedure is painful, and personal choices also meet family expectations about how a woman should look and behave.

Photography has added another use for the plate. Visitors pay women to pose, providing money for goods such as cloth and medicine. Some women assemble more elaborate decorations for these encounters. An appearance tourists treat as evidence of isolation can therefore be part of a relationship with an outside market.

During fieldwork in 2004, anthropologist Shauna LaTosky recorded a disagreement between two other Mursi women. Legessa wanted her lip to shrink. She hoped to study and avoid the ridicule she expected outside Mursi communities. Barmille wanted to keep hers. For her, wearing a lip plate did not prevent education or participation in Ethiopian public life. Discussing Amharic, a language used in government and schooling, she said:

> I can also learn Amharic even if I have a long dangling lip.
meaningBrief: The named portrait offers a starting point for understanding lip plates as a socially meaningful and contested practice. Photography connects this appearance to tourist income. Women’s own differing perspectives complicate the idea that education and cultural belonging require a single choice. Do not attribute those perspectives to Engalo.

sources.title: Joey L.: The Omo Valley portfolio, Portrait of Engalo
sources.supports: Exact identity, Mursi affiliation, Lower Omo Valley location, titled photograph, and published original image. The caption dates the whole series 2008–ongoing; the downloadable image’s embedded original capture date is 19 November 2008. The caption’s speculative slave-raider explanation is not adopted.

sources.title: Melissa Leong: Joey Lawrence on his Ethiopian portrait project
sources.supports: Posed colour portraits and studio lighting; intention to depict the people as living in the same contemporary world as his audience. First-person account originally published by Weekend Post on 13 November 2010.

sources.title: Mursi Online: Lip-plates
sources.supports: Adult identity, individual variation, painful initial stretching, and removability. Its broad statement about freedom from coercion is qualified using LaTosky’s fieldwork.

sources.title: Mursi Online: Body Decoration
sources.role: specialist account of changing appearance and tourist income
sources.supports: Income buys cloth, medicines and other market goods; some decorations are assembled for visitors. Does not establish why Engalo wore these particular white markings.

sources.title: Shauna LaTosky: Reflections on the lip-plates of Mursi women as a source of stigma and self-esteem
sources.role: ethnographic fieldwork and recorded Mursi women’s discussion
sources.supports: Family pressure, divergent choices and the discussion between Legessa and Barmille, especially printed pages 390–392. Direct quotation at page 391. These speakers are not Engalo.

quotationNotes.quote: I can also learn Amharic even if I have a long dangling lip.
quotationNotes.speaker: Barmille, in conversation with Legessa and Shauna LaTosky
quotationNotes.locator: Printed page 391; PDF page 10, zero-based index 9
quotationNotes.context: Barmille defends retaining her lip plate while also claiming educational opportunities. This is independent community context, not a quotation from the sitter.
quotationNotes.translation: English transcription/translation published by Shauna LaTosky; underlying audio not inspected.
quotationNotes.selectionReason: A concrete statement connects cultural self-presentation and schooling without an outsider’s abstract conclusion.
